content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Understand what a translation is and how it moves shapes
Use column vectors to describe translations
Perform translations on a coordinate grid
Describe a translation fully using a column vector
Identify the image of a shape after a translation
Imagine sliding a book across a table without rotating or flipping it. Every point on the book moves the same distance in the same direction. This is a
— one of the four geometric transformations you need to know. Translations appear everywhere: scrolling text on a screen, moving chess pieces in straight lines, or shifting furniture across a room.
is a transformation that moves every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction. The shape does not change size, rotate, or flip.

Every point moves by the same amount
$x$ is the horizontal movement (positive = right, negative = left)
$y$ is the vertical movement (positive = up, negative = down)

Take each vertex (corner) of the shape
Plot the new points and join them up
If a point is at $(x, y)$, after translation by $\binom{a}{b}$ it moves to $(x + a, y + b)$.

Explain why the area of a shape is unchanged after a translation.
The shape moves 3 units to the left and 2 units down.

The perimeter is the same as triangle $ABC$ since translations preserve lengths. $AB = 4$, $AC = \sqrt{4+9} = \sqrt{13}$, $BC = \sqrt{4+9} = \sqrt{13}$. Perimeter $= 4 + 2\sqrt{13} \approx 11.2$ units.
A translation moves every point the same distance in the same direction. The shape is congruent to its image (same shape and size), so the area is preserved.
